segments.translation: [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} tells of that same matter, through the realization of the dharma of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the word “[Ḍombī]{dombi}”:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: through his realization of the dharma of selflessness, Kāṇha tells of that same matter in twilight language, under the word ‘Ḍombī’.

flags.note: nairātmadharma: I render ‘the dharma of selflessness’ and mark it nairatmya, since the short-a compound reads most naturally as the doctrine. The glossary files this form under nairatma (the goddess), and ‘Nairātmā's dharma / nature’ is possible. The instrumental adhigamena could also be ‘by way of’ or ‘with a view to’ the realization.

sandhyābhāsayā for sandhyābhāṣayā (s for ṣ, usual in this manuscript); translated ‘twilight language’ per the glossary. tam evārtham, ‘that same matter’, presumably points back to the theme of the preceding song.

segments.translit: nagarītyādi aspṛśayogatvāt ḍombīti pariśuddhāvadhūtī nairātmā boddhavyā| brahmaṇeti brahmahūṃkārabījajātaṃ capalayogatvāt cittavaṭukaṃ| asampradāyayogināṃ bodhicittaṃ saṃvṛttiśukrarūpaṃ maṇimūlāt viramānandāt spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā gacchasi| bho nairātmā| nagariketi[17]| rūpādiviṣayasamūhaṃ boddhavyaṃ| tasya bāhye| indriyāṇā[m]agocaratvena gurusampradāyāt tavāgāraṃ mahāsukhacakraṃ mayā siddhācāryyeṇa kṛṣṇapādenāvagatamiti|
segments.translation: “Outside the [town]{town}…” and so on. Because she is not to be touched, “[Ḍombī]{dombi}” is to be understood as [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. “[Brahmin]{brahmin}” means the brahmin boy that is the [mind]{citta}: born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which is brahma, and a boy because it is restless. The [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} of [yogis]{yogi} who lack the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, which in [conventional]{samvrti} terms has the form of semen, you touch and touch from the [root of the jewel]{manimula}, the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, and go, O [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. “[Town]{town}” is to be understood as the mass of [sense objects]{visaya} beginning with visible form. Outside it. Your house, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, being beyond the range of the senses, I, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, have come to know through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads Ḍombī as Nairātmā, the purified avadhūtī, called Ḍombī because she cannot be touched; the brahmin as the restless mind, born from the syllable HŪṂ; the town as the mass of sense objects; and her hut outside it as the wheel of great bliss, beyond the senses, which Kāṇha knows through the guru's lineage.

equations.en: Nairātmā, the purified avadhūtī (so called because she is not to be touched)
the mind as a restless brahmin boy (cittavaṭuka), born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which is brahma
the mass of sense objects beginning with visible form
the wheel of great bliss, beyond the range of the senses
the joy of cessation

flags.note: Divergence, not harmonized: Munidatta renders 1b with a second-person verb (spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā gacchasi, ‘you touch and touch and go’) addressed to Nairātmā, so Ḍombī is the one who goes; the song has so bāhma … yāi, ‘that brahmin goes’ (third person). He glosses the brahmin separately as the mind but does not fit it into his sentence. His spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā does support the draft's ‘touching and touching’ for chai choi.

The bodhicitta sentence is loose. I take bodhicittaṃ as object of spṛṣṭvā and the two ablatives (maṇimūlāt viramānandāt) as in apposition, ‘from the root of the jewel, the joy of cessation’; ‘starting from’ is also possible. What her touching and going does to the yogis' bodhicitta is not spelled out.

Minor slips translated through: aspṛśa for aspṛśya; bho nairātmā (nominative) for the vocative nairātme; saṃvṛtti for saṃvṛti. ‘Outside it’ (tasya bāhye) stands as its own clause in the edition; it may run on into the next sentence (‘outside it is your house…’).

brahmahūṃkārabījajātaṃ: I read ‘born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which is (called) brahma’; ‘born from brahma and the HŪṂ seed’ is grammatically possible. vaṭuka is a boy, especially a young brahmin student; I take capalayogatvāt as explaining the ‘boy’. The song's nāṛiā (draft ‘shaven-headed’) is not glossed at all.

segments.translit:
alo ḍombi ityādi| bho ḍombi nairātme tvayā saha mayā abhiṣvaṅgaḥ karttavyaḥ| yādṛśasvabhāvastādṛśo nirghṛṇo lajjādidoṣarahito'ham| tenāhaṃ satataṃ nirantara[ṃ] gṛhītvā prajñopāyātmikāṃ mahāmudrāṃ siddhiṃ labhe|
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
prajñopāyātmakaṃ tantraṃ tanme nigaditaṃ śṛṇu|
segments.translation: “Hey [Ḍombī]{dombi}…” and so on. O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, I must be closely joined with you. As my nature is, so I am: [without disgust]{nirghrna}, free of faults such as shame. So, holding on constantly and without a break, I attain the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}, whose nature is [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}. And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “Hear from me the tantra whose nature is [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, as I declare it.”
segments.note: Munidatta hears Kāṇha address Nairātmā as Ḍombī: he must be closely joined with her. ‘Without disgust’ means free of faults such as shame. Holding on constantly, without a break, he attains the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, whose nature is wisdom and means, words Munidatta echoes from the Hevajra's description of itself.

equations.en: Nairātmā
free of faults such as shame

flags.note: yādṛśasvabhāvas tādṛśo: I read ‘as my nature is, so I am’ (I am as I naturally am, without disgust). It could instead mean ‘of the same nature (as you)’, which would make it Munidatta's gloss on the song's toe sama, ‘with you’. ‘my’ is supplied.

gṛhītvā has no expressed object (presumably Nairātmā, glossing the song's lāga); I leave it implicit as ‘holding on’. abhiṣvaṅgaḥ kartavyaḥ is a gerundive, rendered ‘I must be closely joined’; abhiṣvaṅga can also be ‘embrace’ or ‘clinging’.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsasthānamāha—
eka so ityādi| padmaikaṃ nirmmāṇacakraṃ catuḥṣaṣṭidalayuktaṃ tatra sthitvā bhagavatyā nairātmayā saha ekarasatayā mahārāgānandasundaro hi kṛṣṇācāryyo nṛtyati|
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
nāṭyaṃ kuru herukarūpeṇānusmṛtiśrutiyogataḥ|
segments.translation: With the second verse he states the place of practice: “A single…” and so on. The single [lotus]{lotus} is the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}, with sixty-four petals. Standing there, together with the Blessed Lady [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, in [one taste]{ekarasa}, Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, lovely with the [joy]{ananda} of great passion, dances. And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “Dance in the form of [Heruka]{p-heruka}, by way of recollection and hearing.”
segments.note: Munidatta takes this verse as naming the place of practice. The single lotus is the wheel of emanation, with its sixty-four petals. Where the song has Ḍombī dance, he has Kāṇha himself dance there, in one taste with the Blessed Lady Nairātmā, lovely with the joy of great passion, and cites the Hevajra's call to dance in Heruka's form.

equations.en: the wheel of emanation, with sixty-four petals

flags.note: Divergence, not harmonized: in the song (3b) it is Ḍombī who climbs the lotus and dances; Munidatta says Kṛṣṇācārya dances there with Nairātmā.

Hevajra line: anusmṛtiśrutiyogataḥ is unclear. I render ‘by way of recollection and hearing’; alternatives are ‘through the yoga of recollection and hearing’ or, taking śruti in its musical sense, ‘with recollection, in time with the music’. He names the Hevajra, but I have not placed the line in it.

The edition prints sundarohi; I read sundaro hi (emphatic particle), untranslated. padmaikaṃ = padma ekaṃ, ‘the one lotus’. Pada counting: couplet 1 is the first pada, the refrain is not counted, so this couplet (3) is ‘the second verse’.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena nairātmādhigamaṃ dṛḍhīkaroti| hañcū lo ityādi| bho nairātme sadbhāvena svarūpāśayena tvāṃ pṛcchāmyahaṃ sarvvadharmmanairā[17ka]tmayā kasya saṃvṛttibodhicitta[ttā]naukāmārgeṇa yātāyātaṃ karoṣi na karoṣītyarthaḥ| sarvvasahajamayatveneti|
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
tasmāt sahajaṃ jagat sarvvaṃ sahajaṃ svarūpamucyate|
svarūpameva nirvvāṇaṃ viśuddhākāracetasā||
segments.translation: With the third verse he makes firm the realization of [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. “Hey…” and so on. O [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, I ask you in good faith, that is, with an intention set on the [true nature]{svarupa}: given the [selflessness]{nairatmya} of all phenomena, by way of whose [boat]{boat} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} do you come and go? The sense is: you do not, because all things are made of the [innate]{sahaja}. And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “Therefore the whole world is [innate]{sahaja}; the [innate]{sahaja} is called the [true nature]{svarupa}. The [true nature]{svarupa} itself is [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, for a mind whose aspect is pure.”
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse confirms the realization of Nairātmā. Asking in good faith means asking with intent on the true nature. The boat is conventional bodhicitta; the question ‘in whose boat do you come and go?’ implies she does not, since all phenomena are selfless and everything is made of the innate, as the Hevajra verse says.

equations.en: conventional bodhicitta, by way of which she comes and goes
Nairātmā
an intention set on the true nature

citations.quoted: tasmāt sahajaṃ jagat sarvvaṃ sahajaṃ svarūpamucyate| svarūpameva nirvvāṇaṃ viśuddhākāracetasā||

flags.note: The pratīka reads hañcū lo, which does not match the song's hālo ḍombī (4a); probably a scribal corruption. I translate it as ‘Hey…’ to match the draft.

saṃvṛtibodhicittanaukāmārgeṇa: I read ‘by way of the boat that is conventional bodhicitta’ (boat = bodhicitta, mārgeṇa = ‘by way of’). The glossary's ‘the path of conventional bodhicitta’ is also possible.
svarūpāśayena, glossing sadbhāvena: ‘with an intention set on the true nature’; it could also be simply ‘with genuine intent’ (svarūpa as ‘real, one's own’).

karoṣi na karoṣīty arthaḥ: I take the question as rhetorical, with ‘you do not’ as the sense, supported by the reason that follows (everything is made of the innate). ‘Do you or do you not come and go?’ is a weaker alternative.

bodhicitta[ttā]naukā: Shastri's bracketed ‘ttā’ is unclear (perhaps bodhicittā naukā); it does not change the sense. The edition reads sarvvadharmmanairātmayā (feminine instrumental), rendered ‘the selflessness of all phenomena’.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena nairātmadharmmasvarūpamāha—
tāntītyādi| tantrīti bhagaṃ padmasthānaṃ avidyārūpaṃ| cāṅgitamityādi| tasya pallavaṃ ṣiṣayābhāsaṃ| etayoḥ śrīgurupādaprasādānma(tma)ma vikrayaṇaṃ parityāgaṃ karoṣi(si) bho ḍombi nairātme| ataeva naṭavat saṃsārapeṭakaṃ mayā parityaktaṃ tavāntareṇeti|
segments.translation: With the fourth verse he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of the dharma of [selflessness]{nairatmya}: “[Ḍombī]{dombi} sells [cord]{tanti}…” and so on. “[Cord]{tanti}” means the [bhaga]{bhaga}, the place of the [lotus]{lotus}, which has the form of [ignorance]{avidya}. “…no more baskets…” and so on: its offshoot, the appearance of [sense objects]{visaya}. Through the grace of my revered [guru]{guru}, O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, you sell these two, that is, you give them up. That is why, like a performer, I have given up the basket of [saṃsāra]{samsara} for your sake.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the cord Ḍombī sells as the bhaga, the female organ, place of the lotus, having the form of ignorance; the word for baskets as its offshoot, the appearance of sense objects. By the guru's grace Nairātmā sells, that is, gives up, both; so Kāṇha, like a performer, has given up the basket of saṃsāra.

equations.en: the bhaga, the place of the lotus, which has the form of ignorance
its offshoot (pallava), the appearance of sense objects
giving up
the basket of saṃsāra
Nairātmā

flags.note: Divergence: Munidatta's pratīka is cāṅgitam (song caṅgatā), and he glosses it as pallava, ‘shoot, offshoot, twig’, which does not obviously match the draft's ‘baskets’ (unless he is thinking of wickerwork). I translate his gloss as ‘offshoot’ and quote the draft's wording in the pratīka. The song's abara nā (‘no more’) is not glossed.

prasādānma(tma)ma: I read prasādān mama and take mama with the guru (‘my revered guru’); it could instead go with the verb (‘you sell them for me’). Shastri's parenthesis (tma) suggests a correction to prasādāt mama; either way the sense is close.
ṣiṣayābhāsaṃ is a misprint for viṣayābhāsaṃ (as the glossary notes). karoṣi(si): the parenthesis records the manuscript spelling karosi; translated through.
bhaga kept in source form (proposal below) rather than rendered ‘vulva’ or ‘female organ’; the note glosses it.

segments.translit:
pañcamapadena yogīndrasya saprapañcacaryyāmāha—
tuletyādi| bho ḍombi nairātme svarūpatayā tvāṃ bhadreṇa sadguruprasādāt jānāmi| haum̐ kāpālikaḥ| caryyādharaśca| kaṃ tava sukhaṃ pālituṃ samarthaḥ| ataeva tavāntareṇa mayā kṛṣṇācāryyeṇa ṣaṭtathāgatacakrīkuṇḍalakaṇṭhikādiniraṃśucaryyāṃ(yāṃ) vidhṛtya bāhyamantratantranirapekṣyatayā pañcava[18]rṇṇaviharaṇaṃ kṛtaṃ|
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ—
eku na kkijai manta na tanta
ṇiagharaṇī lai keli karanta|
naa gharem̐ gharaṇī jāva ṇa majjai
tāva ki pañcavāṇṇa viharijjai||
segments.translation: With the fifth verse he states the [conduct]{carya} with elaboration of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}: “You, girl…” and so on. O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, through the grace of the true [guru]{guru} I know you rightly, in your [true nature]{svarupa}. I am a [kāpālika]{kapalika} and one who keeps the [conduct]{carya}: able to guard ka, your bliss. That is why, for your sake, I, Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, have taken up the unclothed [conduct]{carya} with the wheel, earrings, necklace and the rest of the six [tathāgatas]{tathagata}, and, with no regard for outer mantras and tantras, have sported in the five colours. And so the revered Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}: “Not one thing is done, no mantra, no tantra: / taking one's own housewife, one makes love-play. / As long as the housewife in the house is not immersed, / how can one sport in the five colours?”
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse shows the lord of yogis' conduct with elaboration. Knowing Nairātmā truly by the guru's grace, Kāṇha is a kāpālika: one able to guard (pāl-) ka, her bliss. For her sake he adopts the conduct of the six tathāgatas' wheel, earrings and necklace, ignores outer mantras and tantras, and sports in ‘the five colours’.

equations.en: one able to guard ka, that is, your bliss
Nairātmā

citations.quoted: eku na kkijai manta na tanta / ṇiagharaṇī lai keli karanta| / naa gharem̐ gharaṇī jāva ṇa majjai / tāva ki pañcavāṇṇa viharijjai||
citations.work: A dohā of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), perhaps from his Dohākoṣa; Munidatta names the author but not the work

flags.note: niraṃśucaryyāṃ: niraṃśu is not a word as it stands. I take it as niraṃśuka, ‘unclothed’ (the naked conduct with bone ornaments); niraṃśa, ‘partless, undivided (conduct)’, is the other candidate. Probably corrupt.

pañcavarṇa (Apabhraṃśa pañcavāṇṇa), here and in the quoted verse: ‘five colours’ is literal. varṇa also means caste, so ‘roaming among the five castes’ (for example, consorts of five castes) is possible. I kept ‘five colours’ and do not resolve it.
kaṃ tava sukhaṃ pālituṃ samarthaḥ is a folk etymology of kapālī: ka (a lexical word for bliss) + pāl- ‘to guard’. English cannot carry the pun; the note spells it out.

Apabhraṃśa verse: naa gharem̐ may be ṇia ghareṃ, ‘in one's own house’ (matching ṇiagharaṇī), or naa = nava, ‘in the new house’; I wrote the neutral ‘in the house’. majjai, ‘is immersed / sinks / dissolves’, is uncertain in sense. kkijai = kijjai, ‘is done’.

cakrī is the wheel ornament worn on the head; I did not link it to the glossary's ‘wheel’ entry, which is for the song-14 image. nirapekṣyatayā for nirapekṣatayā. The song's ‘garland of bones’ (6b) is not named as such; Munidatta lists wheel, earrings, necklace ‘and the rest’.

segments.translit:
ṣaṣṭhapadena ḍombinīdvidhābhedamāha—
saravaretyādi| gurusampradāyavihīnasya saiva ḍombinī apariśuddhāvadhūtikā sarovaraṃ kāyapuṣkaraṃ tanmūlaṃ tadeva bodhicittaṃ saṃvṛttyā śukrarūpaṃ mārayāmi| niḥsvabhāvīkaromi|
tathā ca bahiśāstre—
śā vittī kimpi jalaṃ yattu viśeṣeṇa gauravaṃ lahei|
ahimuha paḍia garalaṃ cchippi mutānaṃ kuṇeim̐|| 10||
segments.translation: With the sixth verse he states the twofold division of the [Ḍombī]{dombi}: “Breaking the [lake]{lake}…” and so on. For one who lacks the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, that same [Ḍombī]{dombi} is the unpurified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. The [lake]{lake} is the lotus pool of the body. Its root is that very [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, which in [conventional]{samvrti} terms has the form of semen. “I will kill”: I make her without intrinsic nature. And so in an outer treatise: “It is just water, yet by the difference of where it falls it gains its worth: fallen into a snake's mouth it is poison; the oyster shell makes it pearls.”
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse shows that Ḍombī is twofold: for one without the guru's lineage she is the unpurified avadhūtī. The lake is the body as a lotus pool; its root, bodhicitta, conventionally semen. ‘I will kill’ means making her without intrinsic nature. His proverb: the same water becomes poison in a snake's mouth, pearls in an oyster.

equations.en: the unpurified avadhūtī, for one who lacks the guru's lineage
the lotus pool of the body (kāyapuṣkara)
bodhicitta, which in conventional terms has the form of semen
I make (her) without intrinsic nature

citations.quoted: śā vittī kimpi jalaṃ yattu viśeṣeṇa gauravaṃ lahei| ahimuha paḍia garalaṃ cchippi mutānaṃ kuṇeim̐||
citations.work: Unnamed ‘outer treatise’ (bahiḥśāstra); an unidentified Prakrit gnomic verse

flags.note: The Prakrit verse is badly corrupt. My reconstruction: cchippi = sippi, ‘oyster shell’; mutānaṃ = muttāṇaṃ, ‘pearls’; yattu perhaps jattha, ‘where’; śā vittī unclear (perhaps sā vi, ‘that same’). The poison/pearl contrast seems secure; the first line is a guess.

Object of mārayāmi / niḥsvabhāvīkaromi is not expressed. I supply ‘her’ (Ḍombī, as in the song's mārami ḍombī, taking the phrases as a string of glosses). Grammatically the preceding accusative bodhicittaṃ could be the object: ‘I kill that very bodhicitta… I make it without intrinsic nature’.

bahiśāstre (for bahiḥśāstre), ‘in an outer treatise’: a work outside the tantric teaching, here a worldly proverb. The closing ‘|| 10||’ is the song number and is not translated. The song's bhāñjīa (‘breaking’) and khāa (‘eats’) are not glossed.

proposals.definition: The female organ (the word also means ‘good fortune, share’), a frequent term in the yoginī tantras and their commentaries. Munidatta equates the cord Ḍombī sells with the bhaga, ‘the place of the lotus’, which he says has the form of ignorance (cp.10.m6).
proposals.rationale: Occurs as the referent of an image (tanti already forbids it in verse lines) and is likely to recur in Munidatta's glosses; keeping the source word avoids both clinical and coarse English and lets one entry explain it.

proposals.definition: ‘Root of the jewel’: a place in the yogic body; in tantric usage ‘jewel’ (maṇi) commonly denotes the male organ. Munidatta sets it in apposition with the joy of cessation: Nairātmā touches the bodhicitta of yogis without the guru's lineage ‘from the root of the jewel, the joy of cessation’ (cp.10.m2).
proposals.rationale: The glossary's joy-of-cessation entry already refers to it, so it recurs; a fixed English rendering keeps the commentary consistent.

proposals.definition: One's own form: what a thing really is, as against how it appears. Munidatta glosses Kāṇha's ‘in good faith’ as ‘with an intention set on the true nature’ and quotes the Hevajra: the innate is called the true nature, and the true nature itself is nirvāṇa (cp.10.m5).
proposals.rationale: Occurs five times in this song's commentary and is basic to Munidatta's vocabulary; a fixed rendering keeps it distinct from svabhāva (‘nature, intrinsic nature’), which he uses in niḥsvabhāva.

questions: Names: the glossary gives only ‘Kāṇha’ for p-kanha, so I rendered Munidatta's Kṛṣṇapāda as ‘Kāṇha’ and Kṛṣṇācārya as ‘Master Kāṇha’. Should Kṛṣṇapāda and Kṛṣṇācārya be admitted as listed variants so that his Sanskrit forms can stand?

boat: the glossary gives Munidatta's reading as ‘the path of conventional bodhicitta’. The compound saṃvṛtibodhicittanaukāmārgeṇa reads more naturally as ‘by way of the boat that is conventional bodhicitta’. Revise the entry?

Divergences left unharmonized: 1b (Munidatta's ‘you go’, addressed to Nairātmā, against the song's ‘that brahmin goes’); 3b (Kāṇha dances, against Ḍombī dances); 5a (his pallava, ‘offshoot’, against the draft's ‘baskets’). How should these be signalled on the page?

keep-source-first-gloss terms that first occur in the commentary (avadhūtī, Nairātmā, bodhicitta, siddha, Mahāmudrā, tathāgata, and the proposed bhaga) get no first-occurrence note, because the 60-word notes have no room. Where should those glosses go?
nairātmadharma (m1, m6): I marked it as selflessness (nairatmya), though the glossary files the form under nairatma. Which do you prefer?
pañcavarṇa (m7 and Kāṇha's verse): colours or castes? It may deserve an entry once decided.
Draft 1b's ‘shaven-headed’ for nāṛiā: Munidatta does not gloss the word, so he gives the draft no support either way.
